main.title: Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines
main.subtitle: Six specialists behind enemy lines
main.summary: On June 24, 1998 Pyro Studios brought Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines to PC.

cards.heading: Small teams and carefully planned routes
cards.text: Pyro Studios released Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines for PC on June 24, 1998. Players coordinate a small team of specialists through guarded maps. Patrol routes, sightlines and the timing of each move shape the plan. A commando's particular equipment can solve one part of the mission, while another must wait for the right opportunity to cross a watched area.

cards.heading: Six specialists with different equipment
cards.text: Each specialist carries different tools. The Green Beret climbs and moves heavy objects; the Marine dives and pilots boats; the Driver operates vehicles and mounted guns. The Sapper handles explosives and traps, the Sniper attacks from a distance, and the Spy uses enemy uniforms and distractions. The Driver and Sniper can treat injuries. All carry handguns, but sustained gunfire usually puts the team at a severe disadvantage.

cards.heading: Watching patrols and enemy sightlines
cards.text: Guards watch fixed posts or follow patrol routes. The player can display one enemy's field of vision as a green cone, with separate near and far sections. Bodies, footprints and unusual sounds can attract investigation. An alarm can bring more patrols from nearby garrisons, increasing the difficulty; some missions fail immediately if it sounds. Observing these responses helps the player choose when and where to act.

cards.heading: A briefing defines the mission and escape
cards.text: Twenty missions give the player different subsets of the six commandos. A briefing explains the location, objectives and escape plan before control passes to the team. Completing the assignment requires both carrying out its tasks and leaving the area. Losing any commando causes the mission to fail, making each member's safety part of the plan.

main.title: Banjo-Kazooie
main.summary: Banjo-Kazooie is a 1998 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.heading: A bear and a bird search nine worlds
cards.text: Banjo-Kazooie is a 1998 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. Controlling the player characters, the bear Banjo and the bird Kazooie, the player attempts to save Banjo's kidnapped sister Tooty from the witch Gruntilda. The player explores nine nonlinear worlds to gather items and progress. Using Banjo and Kazooie's traversal and combat abilities, they complete challenges such as solving puzzles, jumping over obstacles, and defeating bosses.

cards.heading: From Dream to a platform adventure
cards.text: Rare conceived Banjo-Kazooie as a role-playing video game, Dream, for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System following the completion of Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest (1995). The 15-member team, led by Gregg Mayles, transitioned development to the Nintendo 64 and retooled the game as a platformer after the role-playing format proved too complex. Banjo-Kazooie was inspired by Super Mario 64 (1996) and designed to appeal to a broad audience, similar to Disney films. Grant Kirkhope composed the soundtrack; Banjo-Kazooie was one of the first games to feature vertical remixing, where various sound layers fade in and out depending on the player's location.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Released in North America in late June 1998 and in Europe the following month, Banjo-Kazooie sold over three million copies, making it one of the bestselling Nintendo 64 games. It received acclaim from critics, who said it surpassed Super Mario 64 as the best 3D platform and adventure game. The game was praised for its visuals, soundtrack, characters, writing, humour, and level design, while criticism was directed towards lack of originality and the camera system. Banjo-Kazooie received numerous year-end accolades, including two from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences: "Console Action Game of the Year" and "Outstanding Achievement in Art/Graphics".

cards.heading: Sequels, spin-offs and new platforms
cards.text: In retrospect, Banjo-Kazooie has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. It spawned a series which includes two sequels, Banjo-Tooie (2000) and Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts (2008), and two spin-offs, Grunty's Revenge (2003) and Banjo-Pilot (2005). Following Microsoft's 2002 acquisition of Rare, 4J Studios developed a port for the Xbox 360 in 2008, later included in the Xbox One compilation Rare Replay in 2015. It was released on the Nintendo Switch via the Nintendo Classics service in 2022, marking its first rerelease on a Nintendo console. A new port was released for the Evercade line of systems in 2026.

main.title: Kula World
main.subtitle: A beach ball above the void
main.summary: Kula World is a PlayStation puzzle-platform game by Game Design Sweden AB, first released in Europe on 10 July 1998. The player guides a beach ball around suspended structures, collecting the keys needed to open an exit. Rolling across an edge changes the direction of gravity, turning another side of the same structure into the floor. A small collection of blocks can therefore contain several routes that are difficult to see at once. The game asks the player to understand an object by travelling around it rather than looking at it from one fixed side.

cards.heading: A beach ball above the void
cards.text: Kula World is a PlayStation puzzle-platform game by Game Design Sweden AB, first released in Europe on 10 July 1998. The player guides a beach ball around suspended structures, collecting the keys needed to open an exit. Rolling across an edge changes the direction of gravity, turning another side of the same structure into the floor. A small collection of blocks can therefore contain several routes that are difficult to see at once. The game asks the player to understand an object by travelling around it rather than looking at it from one fixed side.

cards.heading: Turn the structure over in your mind
cards.text: Coins and jewels reward exploration, while new obstacles make a direct route more complicated. Moving platforms, transporters and other devices change what can be reached from a particular position. The player has to connect these possibilities with the ball's changing orientation, remembering where an edge leads after the view has turned. A familiar surface may become useful only after approaching it from elsewhere. The challenge grows through combinations of these rules, so progress depends on building a reliable picture of the whole structure while controlling one small part of it.

cards.heading: A puzzle with several names
cards.text: Collecting fruit can unlock bonus stages, where every block must be activated by rolling across it. These levels give the same movement another objective and encourage a more complete exploration of their shapes. Twice a Man supplied the music, reinforcing the game's unusual atmosphere. North America received it as Roll Away, while the Japanese edition was called KulaQuest. It was Game Design Sweden AB's only video game. Its clear central idea remains distinctive: gravity changes at the edge, and the player's understanding has to turn with the ball.

main.title: Street Fighter Alpha 3
main.summary: Street Fighter Alpha 3, released as Street Fighter Zero 3 in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1998 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.text: Street Fighter Alpha 3, released as Street Fighter Zero 3 in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1998 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the third and final installment in the Street Fighter Alpha series, and runs on the same CP System II hardware as previous Alpha games. Alpha 3 further expanded the playable fighter roster from Street Fighter Alpha 2 and added new features such as selectable fighting styles called "isms".

Alpha 3 has also been released on a variety of home platforms starting with the PlayStation version in 1998, which added an exclusive World Tour mode and brought back even more characters, with further versions on the Dreamcast, Sega Saturn, Game Boy Advance, and PlayStation Portable.

main.title: Deep Fear
main.subtitle: Something inside the research station
main.summary: Deep Fear is System Sacom and Sega's survival horror game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 16 July 1998.

cards.heading: Something inside the research station
cards.text: Deep Fear is System Sacom and Sega's survival horror game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 16 July 1998. John Mayor explores the Big Table, an underwater research facility in the Pacific where an infection transforms staff into hostile creatures. Finding survivors and mission items carries him between sections of the base, while weapons and medical supplies help him withstand the threat. Fixed views of pre-rendered environments frame the three-dimensional characters. The setting gives the familiar search through dangerous rooms another pressure: every part of the station depends on a limited supply of air.

cards.heading: The air is another resource
cards.text: Air in each area decreases over time, and gunfire consumes it more quickly. Air System terminals restore the supply and also serve as save points, making them important destinations when planning a route. Underwater passages require a breathing mask with its own limited reserve. Fighting therefore spends more than ammunition: staying in an encounter can also reduce the time available to escape it. Weapon lockers provide equipment and restocking opportunities, while a separate Special weapon slot allows one powerful additional option to accompany John's regular guns.

cards.heading: Horror beneath the surface
cards.text: The production combines monster designs by Yasushi Nirasawa with music by Kenji Kawai, giving the base's failing systems and transformed inhabitants a strong science-fiction character. Rieko Kodama was among its producers. Exploring the station means tracing practical links between people, equipment and rooms while the infection gradually undermines them. A safe terminal or stocked locker becomes reassuring because it supports the next expedition. The underwater setting makes that dependence tangible: the facility offers shelter from the ocean, yet its own dwindling air and infected occupants make remaining inside increasingly dangerous.

main.title: Brave Fencer Musashi
main.subtitle: Two swords and a changing day
main.summary: On July 16, 1998 Square released Brave Fencer Musashi for PlayStation in Japan.

cards.heading: Square takes an action-RPG route
cards.text: Square released Brave Fencer Musashi for PlayStation in Japan on July 16, 1998. Real-time combat, jumping and three-dimensional exploration take place within a world governed by a day-night cycle. The Fusion ability lets Musashi absorb techniques from enemies, giving him new tools for obstacles and combat. The adventure combines this physical action with towns, characters and puzzles.

cards.heading: Fusion, Lumina and absorbed abilities
cards.text: Musashi is a platform game in which the title character, Musashi, fights a variety of enemies using his swords Fusion and Lumina and searches for five scrolls which will increase Lumina's strength and grant him new abilities. There are also several minigames and puzzles scattered throughout which must be completed to advance the plot. The two swords he uses have varied abilities and uses. Fusion, which resembles a katana, is used to chain rapid combo hits together and can also be used to absorb Bincho energy, which is a type of magical point system that controls how many spells a player can cast and how quickly, or absorb an enemies' skill. Lumina is a large, double-edged weapon which cannot be effectively used in combos by itself; instead, it can be imbued with elemental properties from Scrolls. Lumina is primarily offensive but in combination with the five elemental scrolls, it gains new skills. The two swords can be used in conjunction with certain techniques which are granted by various rescued townsfolk.

cards.heading: Designing a new action role-playing game
cards.text: Executive producer Hironobu Sakaguchi stated that the idea for the game first came up in February 1997. The original idea for Brave Fencer Musashi was having Miyamoto Musashi fighting in an alternate world from where he belonged. While the game was conceptualized as action-oriented, Musashi was originally meant to be a wanderer, but was later changed to an itinerant Samaritan in order to have him interacting and helping other characters. During development, the team used an action base which was crucial to the game's fighting mechanics. Director Yoichi Yoshimoto focused on the game's fully polygonal aspects that were a departure from Square's previous works. The development team prioritized the movement of polygons in real time and how light affected their appearance.

cards.heading: Rest, action figures and new movement abilities
cards.text: The player can either go to an inn to recover Musashi's health or make Musashi sleep outdoors without a full recovery and with danger he may be attacked by enemies. To pass time, the player may also opt to collect the various action figures – which resemble more detailed models of nearly all the characters and monsters – available at the town toy store, which stocks new items at the start of every chapter. Along the way, Musashi obtains parts from the Legendary Armor which allow him to perform actions such as climbing or performing double jumps.

main.title: The King of Fighters '98
main.subtitle: A dream match for the whole cast
main.summary: The King of Fighters '98 is SNK's team fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS on 23 July 1998.

cards.heading: A dream match for the whole cast
cards.text: The King of Fighters '98 is SNK's team fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS on 23 July 1998. After the previous game's conclusion of the Orochi story, it gathers a broad selection of returning fighters for a dream match. Players assemble teams of three, bringing together characters from across the series' first five editions. Rugal returns as the final opponent, while several fighters offer alternative versions with earlier move sets. The emphasis falls on the pleasure and possibilities of the assembled cast, giving the tournament the character of a celebration.

cards.heading: Advance or Extra
cards.text: Two systems, Advance and Extra, provide different ways to manage movement and the power gauge. The choice changes the framework around a fighter's individual moves, allowing the player to favour an approach learned in another entry. Losing a teammate also grants a compensating advantage: Advance increases the remaining capacity for stored power, while Extra makes charging easier and changes access to stronger techniques. A reduced team can therefore retain the means to recover, keeping the later rounds dangerous even after an opponent has established an early lead.

cards.heading: Building a team to return to
cards.text: The roster's breadth gives team construction a lasting purpose. A player can return to favourites, experiment with another order or combine characters whose strengths address different situations. Alternate versions extend that exploration within a familiar face. Director Toyohisa Tanabe and the team considered returning characters with input from players, making the selection part of the game's identity. Later adaptations and Ultimate Match expanded its life, but the original already offered the central attraction: a large, carefully connected fighting cast whose combinations could sustain repeated contests after the story arc had finished.

main.title: SoulCalibur
main.subtitle: Circling the opponent with a weapon
main.summary: On July 30, 1998 Namco released SoulCalibur in arcades.

cards.heading: Eight directions in the arena
cards.text: Namco released SoulCalibur in arcades on July 30, 1998. Its weapon-based fighting uses reach, timing and space to distinguish the cast. The 8-Way Run lets fighters move continuously around one another, making position within the arena important. A later Dreamcast conversion expanded the game and helped establish its wider reputation.

cards.heading: Moving around an opponent
cards.text: One of the biggest innovations introduced by Soulcalibur to the gameplay system of its predecessor, Soul Edge, is the eight-way run. Previous 3D fighters had only limited movement along the third axis, with sidesteps and rolls providing useful but unsustained lateral movement. In Soulcalibur, simply holding down a joystick direction causes the character to move in that direction, giving the player a sense of freedom and deepening the strategy of the game.

cards.heading: Designing each fighter around a weapon
cards.text: Yotoriyama described the concept as finding variety and enjoyment in weapon combat. Each fighter's movements were built around a particular weapon, creating differences in reach and timing that also made balancing difficult. Movement interacted with the possibility of a ring-out. Motion creator Masataka Ishiguro emphasised arm and leg actions appropriate to each weapon so players could recognise the distinct fighting styles.

cards.heading: The expanded Dreamcast version
cards.text: The Dreamcast conversion improved the graphics with three-dimensional backgrounds and added costumes, modes and Cervantes de Leon. Team Battle, Survival and Training offered different ways to play. Mission Battle awarded points for tasks, letting players buy artwork and unlock further features, costumes and stages. Exhibition sequences showed fighters performing their katas, while other unlocks could change the introduction or presentation.

main.title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six
main.summary: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six is a 1998 tactical shooter video game developed and published by Red Storm Entertainment for Microsoft Windows, with later ports for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Mac OS, Game Boy Color, and Dreamcast.

cards.heading: A counterterrorist team on the original PC
cards.text: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six is a 1998 tactical shooter video game developed and published by Red Storm Entertainment for Microsoft Windows, with later ports for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Mac OS, Game Boy Color, and Dreamcast. It is the first installment in the Rainbow Six series. Based on the Tom Clancy novel of the same name, the game follows Rainbow, a top secret international counterterrorist organization, and the conspiracy they unravel as they handle a seemingly random spike in terrorism.

cards.heading: Planning, teams and tactical decisions
cards.text: In singleplayer, the player advances through a series of missions in a campaign. Before each mission, the player is briefed on the situation, selects and organizes their operatives and equipment, and plans their movement through the level; during missions, the player controls an operative leading computer-controlled teammates as they follow the player's plan. In multiplayer, players cooperate in player-versus-environment missions or battle to complete objectives in player-versus-player matches. The game features realistic gameplay factors, weapon lethality, and consequences for failure, forcing players to plan their approach carefully and promoting replayability for more streamlined completion.

cards.heading: Developing realism alongside the novel
cards.text: Rainbow Six began as a concept by Red Storm following their formation in 1996. The game was developed in parallel with the Rainbow Six novel, with a design philosophy of realism and strategy guiding all aspects of development; however, numerous setbacks stymied the game's development and forced the developers to crunch. Though his name is in the game's title, Tom Clancy's involvement in Rainbow Six's development was very minimal. Red Storm developed the PC version, while all other ports were developed by their respective companies.

cards.heading: A tactical shooter and its reception
cards.text: Rainbow Six was released on August 21, 1998 to widespread critical acclaim, though the console ports received relatively lower ratings than the PC version. For most releases, praise was directed toward gameplay, multiplayer, immersion, and the game's combination of strategy and action, while criticism mainly centered on AI issues, glitches, and the graphics and controls of some ports. The game sold over 200,000 copies in its first year of release and continued to sell hundreds of thousands more copies well into the early 2000s. Rainbow Six was nominated for numerous accolades and has been deemed one of the best video games of 1998. It is considered a milestone in the history of first-person shooters and made a lasting impact on the then-fledgling tactical shooter genre.

cards.heading: Eagle Watch and the following games
cards.text: An expansion pack, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Mission Pack: Eagle Watch, was released on January 26, 1999. A sequel, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear, was released in 1999. A loose mobile game remake, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Shadow Vanguard, was released in 2011.

main.title: Metal Gear Solid
main.subtitle: Infiltrating Shadow Moses
main.summary: Konami released Metal Gear Solid in Japan for PlayStation on September 3, 1998.

cards.heading: Stealth reaches three dimensions
cards.text: Konami released Metal Gear Solid for PlayStation in Japan on September 3, 1998. Hideo Kojima's stealth series moved into three dimensions, with Solid Snake infiltrating Shadow Moses. Camera views, radar, sound and codec conversations supply information about the mission and its dangers. Boss encounters also use the player's relationship with the console and controller as part of their design.

cards.heading: Reading the Soliton radar
cards.text: The Soliton radar shows guards and their fields of vision, including threats outside the camera's immediate view. Players compare it with the room around Snake to find a safe route. When an alert begins, the radar changes state, reducing the information available at a dangerous moment. The relationship between the two views makes observation part of moving through the base.

cards.heading: Conversations over the codec
cards.text: Snake can contact Colonel Campbell, Naomi, Mei Ling and others over the codec. Two portraits and a voice conversation interrupt the pace of infiltration to supply instructions, background, jokes or doubts about the mission. These exchanges let the story expand while Snake remains in the same location, giving him a support network during otherwise solitary fieldwork.

cards.heading: Psycho Mantis uses the console
cards.text: Psycho Mantis comments on information found on the Memory Card and seems to anticipate the player's inputs. Solving the encounter involves the controller port, bringing the physical PlayStation into the scene. A fight within the base therefore also asks the player to reconsider how they are interacting with the console itself.

features.title: Looking through a miniature room
features.summary: Kojima and Shinkawa negotiated what players could see.

cards.heading: A doorway disappears behind a column
cards.text: During Metal Gear Solid's development, a floor plan could hide problems that appeared only from a character's viewpoint. Kojima described columns concealing doorways that had seemed visible on graph paper. The team built structures from toy blocks and examined them with a miniature camera, testing how the rooms would look from inside before completing their digital versions.

cards.heading: Suspense has an unseen source
cards.text: In a prerelease interview, Kojima recalled being frightened in other games by the sound of crushed leaves without knowing its source. He wanted sound to create similar suspense in Metal Gear Solid. An unseen noise could leave the player uncertain whether it was safe to move, complementing the information provided or withheld by the camera.

cards.heading: The artist builds a physical machine
cards.text: Yoji Shinkawa built a physical model of Metal Gear REX while computer artists developed its digital counterpart. Kojima recalled requesting a machine that suggested a dinosaur when operating. The model gave the team a concrete reference as the design developed, allowing the physical and computer versions to inform one another.

cards.heading: A drawing changes the cast
cards.text: Shinkawa first imagined the cyborg ninja as an ordinary enemy soldier. His drawings changed the idea's role, and the character became important to the story. Kojima recalled adjusting plans around the artist's contribution. A proposed design could therefore affect the cast and narrative as well as the appearance of an enemy.
